blocks.text: Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state (HHS) is an acute, life-threatening complication of diabetes mellitus characterised by severe hyperglycaemia, increased plasma osmolality, profound dehydration and variable neurological impairment, usually without significant ketoacidosis.
It occurs predominantly in patients with type 2 diabetes, particularly older adults, but can also occur in children and adolescents.
HHS is associated with substantial mortality, especially when diagnosis and treatment are delayed or when serious precipitating illnesses are present.

blocks.title: The fundamental difference between DKA and HHS:

items.text: DKA: Significant ketonaemia and metabolic acidosis are central features.
HHS: Severe hyperglycaemia, hyperosmolality and dehydration predominate, with absent or mild ketosis and no significant ketoacidosis.

blocks.text: HHS requires careful fluid replacement, electrolyte management, insulin when indicated, and treatment of the underlying precipitating condition.

blocks.title: HHS is a metabolic emergency characterised by:

blocks.text: There is usually enough residual endogenous insulin activity to suppress extensive lipolysis and ketogenesis, but insufficient insulin to prevent severe hyperglycaemia.

blocks.text: Unlike DKA, patients with HHS generally retain enough endogenous insulin to suppress excessive lipolysis and ketone formation.
However, insulin activity remains insufficient to control hepatic glucose production and peripheral glucose utilisation.

blocks.text: Adult HHS treatment differs from DKA in one important respect: fluid replacement is the initial priority, and insulin is generally started more cautiously.
Rapid insulin administration can cause a dangerous fall in glucose and osmolality, leading to fluid shifts and neurological complications.
First-line intervention
The primary objective is to restore circulating volume, improve renal perfusion and gradually reduce hyperosmolality.

Paediatric HHS is uncommon but particularly dangerous. Children may develop profound dehydration, severe electrolyte depletion, rhabdomyolysis, acute kidney injury and circulatory collapse.
Unlike paediatric DKA, HHS often requires more aggressive initial volume replacement because of the greater degree of fluid depletion.
All children with HHS require urgent paediatric specialist involvement and management in a paediatric intensive care unit or equivalent monitored setting.

subsections.subsection_title: 11. Renal and hepatic impairment, pregnancy and breastfeeding

blocks.text: Renal impairment is common in severe HHS because of dehydration and reduced renal perfusion.

items.text: Adjust fluid replacement to avoid overload.
Consider renal replacement therapy when indicated.

blocks.text: Patients with end-stage kidney disease:
These patients may have different fluid requirements because they cannot excrete excess fluid normally.
Avoid automatically applying standard HHS fluid volumes. Use smaller fluid boluses and frequent haemodynamic reassessment.
Liver disease may affect glucose regulation and insulin metabolism.
Use cautious insulin adjustment and monitor glucose frequently.
HHS during pregnancy is uncommon but constitutes a serious maternal and fetal emergency.

items.text: Frequent maternal glucose and osmolality monitoring.
Fetal monitoring appropriate to gestational age.

blocks.text: Pregnancy-specific DKA/HHS protocols should be used. Avoid overly rapid correction of maternal hyperosmolality.
HHS itself does not permanently prevent breastfeeding.

blocks.text: Essential examination and prescribing points

items.text: HHS is characterised by severe hyperglycaemia, hyperosmolality and dehydration.
Adult glucose diagnostic threshold is ≥600 mg/dL.
Effective osmolality is calculated without urea.
Fluid replacement is the initial treatment priority.
Fluid replacement alone can significantly reduce glucose.
Adult IV insulin is generally started at 0.05 units/kg/hour.
Mixed DKA/HHS requires the DKA insulin regimen.
Glucose should not fall faster than 90–120 mg/dL/hour in adults.
Sodium decline should not exceed 10 mmol/L in 24 hours.
Paediatric HHS may require a 12–15% estimated fluid deficit calculation.
Paediatric insulin is delayed until glucose no longer falls adequately with fluids alone.
Rhabdomyolysis is an important paediatric complication.
HHS can occur with mixed DKA features.
Normalisation of glucose alone does not establish HHS resolution.

rows: Osmolality below 300, glucose below 250, urine output above 0.5 mL/kg/hour and improved cognition
